content: 1. A cluster-randomized trial was conducted to evaluate an intervention aimed at preventing intimate partner violence and reducing HIV risk in rural South Africa. The findings were published in The Lancet in 2006, volume 368, issue 9551, pages 1973–1983. 2. Abramsky and colleagues implemented a community mobilization intervention to prevent violence against women and reduce HIV/AIDS risk in Kampala, Uganda. This was part of the SASA. Trials, with results published in 2012, volume 13, page 96. 3. Hirani and colleagues tested a community-derived intervention to promote women's health in Karachi, Pakistan. Preliminary results from a three-arm randomized controlled trial were accessed online on December 21, 2015. 4. Karmaliani and colleagues applied community-based participatory research methods to improve maternal and child health in Karachi, Pakistan. Their findings were published in Nursing Outlook in 2009, volume 57, issue 4, pages 204–209. 5. Weijer and colleagues developed the Ottawa Statement, which outlines ethical guidelines for the design and conduct of cluster-randomized trials. This was published in PLOS Medicine in 2012, volume 9, issue 11, article e1001346. The statement includes ethical and safety recommendations for research on violence against women. 6. Saftlas and colleagues conducted a randomized trial to evaluate the use of motivational interviewing in addressing intimate partner violence. The results were published in Annals of Epidemiology in 2014, volume 24, issue 2, pages 144–150. 7. García-Moreno and colleagues reported on the prevalence of intimate partner violence based on findings from the WHO multi-country study on women's health and domestic violence. The study was published in The Lancet in 2006, volume 368, issue 9543, page 1260. 8. Altarac and Strobino examined the relationship between abuse during pregnancy, stress, and birth weight. Their findings were published in the Journal of the American Medical Women’s Association in 2002, volume 57, issue 4, pages 208–214. 9. Janssen and colleagues conducted a population-based study on the association between intimate partner violence and adverse pregnancy outcomes. The study was published in American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology in 2003, volume 188, issue 5, pages 1341–1347. 10. Valladares and colleagues identified physical partner abuse during pregnancy as a risk factor for low birth weight in Nicaragua. Their findings were published in Obstetrics and Gynecology in 2002, volume 100, issue 4, pages 700–705. 11. Jejeebhoy explored the associations between wife-beating and fetal and infant death based on a survey conducted in rural India. The findings were published in 1998, page 3008. 12. McFarlane and colleagues investigated the link between abuse during pregnancy and femicide, emphasizing the urgent implications for women's health. Their study was published in Obstetrics and Gynecology in 2002, volume 100, issue 1, pages 27–36. 13. Dunkle and colleagues studied the relationship between gender-based violence, relationship power, and the risk of HIV infection in women attending antenatal clinics in South Africa. The findings were published in The Lancet in 2004, volume 363, issue 9419, pages 1415–1421. 14. Maman and colleagues reported that HIV-positive women experience higher rates of lifetime partner violence. This was based on findings from a voluntary counseling and testing clinic in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, published in American Journal of Public Health in 2002, volume 92, issue 8, pages 1331–1337. 15. Schechter and Edleson provided guidelines for effective intervention in cases of woman battering and child maltreatment. These guidelines were published by the National Council of Juvenile and Family Court Judges in Reno, Nevada, in 1999. 16. Abrahams and colleagues conducted a systematic review on the global prevalence of non-partner sexual violence. The findings were published in The Lancet in 2014, volume 383, issue 9929, pages 1648–1654. 17. The World Health Organization published a report in 2013 on global and regional estimates of violence against women, focusing on the prevalence and health effects of intimate partner violence and non-partner sexual violence. 18. An executive order was issued in 2012 to prevent and respond to violence against women and girls globally. The document was accessed online on December 21, 2015. 19. The United States Department of State and USAID released a strategy in 2012 to prevent and respond to gender-based violence globally. 20. The UK government published an action plan in 2013 titled A Call to End Violence Against Women and Girls, outlining measures to address this issue.
